summary: One spelling with two families of words. The verb זָרַע is to sow, and its noun זֶרַע is what is sown: the seed of plants, the season of sowing, a man's seed, and above all offspring, a man's descendants as one body. Scripture's great promises are made to a seed: the woman's seed who strikes the serpent's head (Gen 3:15), Abraham's seed in whom the nations are blessed (Gen 22:18), which Paul reads as Christ and those in him (Gal 3:16, 29), and David's seed whose throne stands for ever (2Sa 7:12–16). The noun זְרוֹעַ is the arm, and so strength; “the arm of Yahweh” is his own power stretched out to save, revealed in his servant (Isa 53:1; Jhn 12:38). Arabic keeps the two apart, zaraʿa “sow” with z and ḏirāʿ “arm” with ḏ, while Aramaic and Syriac write the arm with d and the seed mostly with z.

words.gloss: seed; sowing, seedtime; semen; offspring, descendants
words.summary: About 230 times. Singular in form even where it means many: a whole line of descendants is one seed, so that the word can stand for a people or for one son (Gen 4:25; 21:13). Most uses are “offspring”, in the promises to the fathers and to David, in genealogy and in the law of the priests.

senses.definition: The seed a plant bears and a farmer sows: the seed of herb and tree, the grain kept for sowing, the bag of seed carried to the field.

evidence.note: “Herb yielding seed (מַזְרִיעַ זֶרַע), fruit tree bearing fruit after its kind, whose seed (זַרְעוֹ) is in it.”
Every herb and tree “bearing seed” given for food.
Joseph: “here is seed for you, and you shall sow the ground (הֵא־לָכֶם זֶרַע וּזְרַעְתֶּם)”.
Four parts kept “for seed of the field and for your food”.
A field valued by its seed: “a homer of barley seed at fifty shekels of silver”.
Egypt, “where you sowed your seed and watered it with your foot”.
The rain makes the earth bring forth “and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater”: seed set beside bread.
He goes out weeping, “carrying the bag of seed (מֶשֶׁךְ־הַזָּרַע)”, and comes back with his sheaves.
“In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not withhold your hand.”
“Is the seed yet in the barn?”
“You shall carry much seed out into the field and gather little, for the locust shall consume it.”
Sowing seed (זֶרַע זֵרוּעַ) touched by a carcass stays clean.
The wilderness “is no place of seed, or fig, or vine, or pomegranate”.

senses.definition: What grows from the seed sown: the year's crop, of which a tithe was taken.

evidence.note: “You shall surely tithe all the produce of your seed (תְּבוּאַת זַרְעֶךָ) that comes out of the field year by year.”
“All the tithe of the land, of the seed of the land, of the fruit of the tree, is Yahweh's.”
The king “will take the tenth of your seed and of your vineyards”.
“The seed of Shihor, the harvest of the Nile, was her revenue.”

senses.definition: The act or season of sowing, set beside harvest in the year's round.

evidence.note: “While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest (זֶרַע וְקָצִיר), cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall not cease.”
“Your threshing shall reach to the vintage, and the vintage shall reach to the sowing time (זָרַע).”

senses.definition: A man's seed, in the law of uncleanness and of marriage: the “lying of seed” (שִׁכְבַת זֶרַע), and a wife's conceiving.

evidence.note: “If a man's lying of seed (שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע) goes out from him, he shall bathe all his flesh in water.”
“You shall not give your lying for seed to your neighbour's wife.”
The wife found clean “shall be free, and shall be sown with seed (וְנִזְרְעָה זָרַע)”: she shall conceive.
Onan spilled it on the ground “so as not to give seed to his brother”.

senses.definition: A man's or woman's children and their line after them, counted as one: a single son, a family, a nation. The covenants are made with a man “and with your seed after you”.

evidence.note: “Between your seed and her seed; he (הוּא) shall strike your head”: the seed is a line, and one of it strikes.
Eve names Seth, “for God has appointed me another seed (זֶרַע אַחֵר) instead of Abel”: one son is a seed.
Abram: “to me you have given no seed, and a son of my house is my heir”.
Ishmael: “I will make him a nation, because he is your seed.”
Judah to Onan: “raise up seed for your brother (וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ)”.
Hannah asks “a seed of men (זֶרַע אֲנָשִׁים)”, a son.
Eli: “Yahweh give you seed of this woman.”
“Your house like the house of Perez … of the seed which Yahweh shall give you of this young woman.”
“I establish my covenant with you and with your seed after you.”
Phinehas: “to him and to his seed after him the covenant of an everlasting priesthood”.
“A man of your seed throughout their generations who has a blemish shall not approach.”
“I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.”
As the new heavens and new earth stand, “so shall your seed and your name stand”.

senses.gloss: the seed of the promise (to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob)
senses.definition: The seed to whom Yahweh promised the land, the multitude like the stars and the sand, and the blessing of the nations; called in Isaac.

evidence.note: “To your seed I will give this land.”
“All the land which you see, to you I will give it, and to your seed for ever.”
“I will make your seed as the dust of the earth.”
“Count the stars … so shall your seed be”: quoted Rom 4:18.
“Your seed shall be a sojourner in a land not theirs”: quoted Act 7:6.
“An everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your seed after you.”
The covenant with Isaac “for an everlasting covenant for his seed after him”.
“In Isaac shall seed be called to you”: quoted Rom 9:7; Heb 11:18.
“I will multiply your seed as the stars of the heavens … and your seed shall possess the gate of his enemies (אֹיְבָיו).”
“In your seed shall all the nations of the earth bless themselves”: quoted Act 3:25; Gal 3:16.
To Jacob: “in you and in your seed shall all the families of the ground be blessed”.
“Israel my servant … the seed of Abraham my friend.”
“Not ‘to seeds’, as of many, but as of one, ‘and to your seed’, which is Christ.”

senses.gloss: royal line; the seed of David
senses.definition: The line of a king, “the seed of the kingdom”; above all David's seed, whom Yahweh promised to raise up and whose throne he would establish for ever.

evidence.note: “I will raise up your seed after you, who shall come out of your body, and I will establish his kingdom.”
“Your seed I will establish for ever, and build up your throne for all generations.”
“His seed shall be for ever, and his throne as the sun before me.”
Covenant faithfulness “to his anointed, to David and to his seed for ever”.
Of Coniah: “no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting on the throne of David”.
“So will I multiply the seed of David my servant.”
Yahweh will not cast away the seed of David “from taking of his seed rulers over the seed of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob”.
Athaliah “destroyed all the seed of the kingdom (זֶרַע הַמַּמְלָכָה)”.
Ishmael “of the seed of the kingdom (מִזֶּרַע הַמְּלוּכָה)”.
In the parable the eagle “took of the seed of the land”, a king's son, and planted it.
God's son “made of the seed of David according to the flesh”.

senses.gloss: a seed marked by its character (holy seed, seed of evildoers)
senses.definition: A people named by what it is, as a son takes after his father: a holy seed, a seed blessed of Yahweh, a seed of evildoers or of falsehood.

evidence.note: “A sinful nation … a seed of evildoers, sons that deal corruptly.”
“Are you not children of transgression, a seed of falsehood?”
“The seed of evildoers shall never be named.”
After the felling, “the holy seed (זֶרַע קֹדֶשׁ) is its stump”.
“The holy seed has mingled itself with the peoples of the lands.”
All who see them shall acknowledge “that they are the seed which Yahweh has blessed”.
“They are the seed of the blessed of Yahweh, and their offspring with them.”
God made them one, “seeking a seed of God”.
“A seed shall serve him.”
The servant, when his soul is made a guilt offering, “shall see seed”.

evidence.locator: Gen.3.15 זַרְעֲךָ → σπέρματος; Gen.12.7 → σπέρματί; Gen.22.18 בְזַרְעֲךָ → σπέρματί; 2Sa.7.12 → σπέρμα; σπέρμα renders זֶרַע ×168

evidence.note: “Not ‘and to seeds (σπέρμασιν)’, as of many, but as of one, ‘and to your seed (σπέρματί)’, which is Christ.”
Gen 22:18 quoted: “in your seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed”.
Gen 21:12 quoted: “in Isaac shall your seed be called”; also Heb 11:18.
Gen 15:5 quoted: “so shall your seed be”.
Gen 15:13 quoted: “his seed should sojourn in a strange land”.
“Has not the scripture said that the Christ comes of the seed of David?”
Gen 38:8 and the law of the brother: “raise up seed for his brother”.
Isa 55:10: he who supplies “seed (σπέρμα) to the sower and bread for food” will multiply “your seed for sowing (σπόρον)”.
“The seed (σπόρος) is the word of God.”

parallels.note: “Offspring, issue”, what comes out of a man: the regular partner of זֶרַע.

evidence.note: “Your seed would have been as the sand, and the offspring of your body like its grains.”
“I will pour my spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring.”

parallels.note: “Name”: a man lives on in his seed and his name.
“Fruit”: children as the fruit of a man.

evidence.note: “Their fruit you will destroy from the earth, and their seed from among the sons of man.”
“The sons of your servants shall dwell, and their seed shall be established before you.”

opposites.note: “Harvest”: seedtime and harvest, the two ends of the farmer's year.

phrases.gloss: lying of seed, emission of seed
your seed after you: the heirs of a covenant
raise up seed (for a dead brother)
the royal seed, the king's family
holy seed: Israel as set apart

words.gloss: sow; (niphal) be sown, conceive; (hiphil) yield seed, conceive
words.summary: About 56 times, nearly all qal, sowing a field or seed. Some forms the brief counts here are the noun זֶרַע by spelling (Gen 15:3; 21:12; Lev 15:16 and others); they are entered under the noun. Its figurative uses carry the farmer's law into conduct: what is sown is reaped.

stems.gloss: sow (seed, a field); scatter (people); (participle) sower; (of plants) yield seed

senses.definition: To scatter seed on ground prepared for it, or to sow a field with seed; the first work of the farmer's year, before reaping.

evidence.note: “Isaac sowed (וַיִּזְרַע) in that land, and found in that year a hundredfold, and Yahweh blessed him.”
“Six years you shall sow your land and gather in its produce.”
In the seventh year “your field you shall not sow, and your vineyard you shall not prune”.
“What shall we eat in the seventh year? We shall not sow nor gather in our produce.”
“You shall not sow your field with two kinds of seed.”
The firstfruits “of your labours which you sow in the field”.
“Does the plowman plow all day to sow?”
“In the third year sow and reap, and plant vineyards and eat their fruit.”
The Rechabites: “you shall not build a house, nor sow seed, nor plant a vineyard”.
“He who watches the wind will not sow.”
The participle: “seed to the sower (לַזֹּרֵעַ)”.
“Cut off the sower from Babylon.”
The wilderness, “a land not sown (לֹא זְרוּעָה)”.
Of plants, “every herb yielding seed (זֹרֵעַ זֶרַע)”.
Abimelech razed Shechem “and sowed it with salt”: sowing that makes the land barren.

senses.gloss: sow and not reap (the curse of the covenant)
senses.definition: Sowing whose harvest another eats or which yields nothing: the covenant's curse on the disobedient.

evidence.note: “You shall sow your seed in vain, for your enemies shall eat it.”
“You shall sow, but not reap.”
“You have sown much and bring in little.”
“They have sown wheat and reaped thorns.”
Job's oath: “let me sow, and another eat”.
“When Israel had sown, Midian came up.”

senses.definition: To sow righteousness or wickedness, trouble or the wind: conduct as seed whose harvest returns on the sower.

evidence.note: “They sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind.”
“Sow for yourselves in righteousness; reap according to covenant faithfulness.”
“He who sows iniquity shall reap calamity.”
“Those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap it.”
“He who sows righteousness, a true reward.”
“Those who sow in tears shall reap with a joyful shout.”
“Light is sown (זָרֻעַ) for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart.”

senses.gloss: sow (a people in the land, among the nations)
senses.definition: Yahweh sows his people as seed: scattering them among the nations, or planting them again in the land to grow and live.

evidence.note: “I will sow her for myself in the land, and I will have mercy on Lo-ruhamah, and say to Lo-ammi, You are my people”: the meaning of Jezreel; quoted Rom 9:25.
“I will sow them among the peoples, and in far countries they shall remember me, and they shall live with their children and return.”
“I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and the seed of beast.”

stems.gloss: be sown; (of a woman) conceive; (of a name) have offspring

senses.definition: Of ground or seed: to be sown.

evidence.note: A valley “which is neither worked nor sown”.
The cursed land, “it is not sown, nor does it bear”.
To the mountains of Israel: “you shall be tilled and sown”.

senses.definition: Of a wife: to be sown with seed, to conceive.

evidence.note: “She shall be free, and shall be sown with seed (וְנִזְרְעָה זָרַע).”

senses.gloss: (of a name) be sown, have descendants
senses.definition: That a man's name be sown is that he have descendants to carry it.

evidence.note: To Nineveh's king: “no more of your name shall be sown”: you shall have no posterity.

senses.definition: Of princes and judges, as plants scarcely rooted.

evidence.note: “Scarcely are they planted, scarcely are they sown (זֹרָעוּ), scarcely has their stock taken root in the earth.”

senses.definition: Of herbs: to produce seed.

evidence.note: “Herb yielding seed (מַזְרִיעַ זֶרַע).”

senses.definition: Of a woman: to conceive and bear.

evidence.note: “If a woman conceives (תַזְרִיעַ) and bears a male child.”

evidence.locator: Isa.55.10 לַזֹּרֵעַ → σπείροντι; Psa.126.5 הַזֹּרְעִים → σπείροντες; Hos.10.12 זִרְעוּ → σπείρατε; forms of σπείρω render about 40 of the verb's tokens

evidence.note: Isa 55:10: “he who supplies seed to the sower (τῷ σπείροντι)”.
“Whatever a man sows, that he shall also reap”: the law of Hos 8:7 and Pro 22:8.
“He who sows sparingly shall reap sparingly.”
“Behold, the sower went out to sow.”
Of the dead: “it is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption”.

parallels.note: “Plant”: sowing the field beside planting the vineyard.
“Plow”: the work that goes before sowing.

opposites.note: “Reap”: the end of what was sown.

words.gloss: arm; shoulder (of a sacrifice); strength, power; (plural) forces
words.summary: About 90 times, also written זְרֹעַ. The arm of the body, and so a man's strength, and Yahweh's own power put forth. Its cognates (Arabic ḏirāʿ, Ugaritic ḏrʿ, Aramaic and Syriac dərāʿā) show an older ḏ behind the ז, where Arabic zaraʿa “sow” shows z: the arm may be a second root that fell together with “sow” in Hebrew spelling. The cognates of “sow” that show z (Arabic, Syriac, the Targums’ זְרַע) therefore count against it in lexicon-support: that is the mark of the split, not evidence against the sense “arm”, which every language with the ḏ form shares.

senses.definition: The arm of a man or woman: bound with ropes, wearing a bracelet, bending a bow, reaping, bearing a seal.

evidence.note: Samson “broke them from off his arms like a thread”.
“The ropes that were on his arms became as flax burnt with fire.”
“The crown that was on his head and the bracelet that was on his arm.”
Jehu shot Joram “between his arms”.
“He teaches my hands to war, so that my arms bend a bow of bronze.”
“As when the reaper gathers the standing grain, and his arm reaps the ears.”
“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.”
“She girds her loins with strength and strengthens her arms.”
The man in linen: “his arms and his feet like burnished bronze”.

senses.definition: The foreleg of the ram or ox, the priest's portion.

evidence.note: At the Nazirite's completion “the priest shall take the boiled shoulder (הַזְּרֹעַ) of the ram”.
The priests' due from a sacrifice: “the shoulder, the two cheeks and the stomach”.

senses.definition: A man's or a nation's might, which can be broken or strengthened; to trust in man is to make flesh one's arm.

evidence.note: To Eli: “I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father's house, that there shall not be an old man in your house”.
“Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from Yahweh.”
Hezekiah: “with him is an arm of flesh, but with us is Yahweh our God”.
“The man of arm (אִישׁ זְרוֹעַ), the earth was his.”
“Break the arm of the wicked.”
“The arms of the wicked shall be broken, but Yahweh upholds the righteous.”
“The high arm is broken.”
“The horn of Moab is cut off, and his arm is broken.”
“I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt.”
“I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon … and break Pharaoh's arms.”
“I strengthened their arms, yet they devise evil against me.”
“Their own arm did not save them, but your right hand and your arm.”
Assyria “has been an arm to the children of Lot”: a help in war.

senses.definition: In Daniel's vision the arms of a king are his forces.

evidence.note: “The arms of the south shall not stand.”
“Arms shall stand from him, and they shall profane the sanctuary.”

senses.gloss: the arm of Yahweh: his power put forth
senses.definition: Yahweh's own strength stretched out to act: in creation, in bringing Israel out of Egypt, in judgment, and in the salvation he works when there is no man to help, which is revealed in his servant.

evidence.note: “I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments.”
“By the greatness of your arm they are as still as a stone.”
“Yahweh brought us out of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm.”
“You have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and your outstretched arm.”
Against Jerusalem: “I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and a strong arm”.
“I will gather you out of the countries … with a strong hand and an outstretched arm.”
“The Lord Yahweh comes with strength, and his arm rules for him.”
“He shall gather the lambs with his arm.”
“Awake, awake, put on strength, arm of Yahweh.”
“Yahweh has bared his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.”
“To whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed?”: quoted Jhn 12:38.
“He saw that there was no man … so his own arm brought salvation to him.”
“Yahweh has sworn by his right hand and by the arm of his strength.”
“His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him.”
“You have an arm with might.”
“With your arm you redeemed your people.”
“Underneath are the everlasting arms.”
“I taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by their arms.”
“Have you an arm like God?”
“He has shown strength with his arm.”
“With a high arm he brought them out of it.”

evidence.locator: Isa.53.1 זְרוֹעַ → βραχίων; Exo.6.6 בִּזְרוֹעַ → βραχίονι; βραχίων renders זְרוֹעַ ×40

evidence.note: Isa 53:1 quoted: “to whom has the arm (ὁ βραχίων) of the Lord been revealed?”
The exodus “with a high arm (μετὰ βραχίονος ὑψηλοῦ)”, the arm of Exo 6:6 and Deu 26:8.
Mary: “he has shown strength with his arm (ἐν βραχίονι αὐτοῦ)”.

parallels.note: “Hand”: the strong hand and the outstretched arm.

phrases.gloss: with a strong hand and an outstretched arm
an arm of flesh: human strength
break the arm: destroy one's power

words.summary: A form of זְרוֹעַ with a prefixed א, twice; Jewish Aramaic has the same form, אֶדְרַע, beside דְּרַע, as Ezra's Aramaic has אֶדְרָע. Like זְרוֹעַ, its balance is lowered by the z cognates of “sow”, another older root.

senses.definition: In the formula of the exodus.

evidence.note: “With a strong hand and with an outstretched arm (וּבְאֶזְרוֹעַ נְטוּיָה) and with great terror.”

senses.definition: Job's own arm, in his oath.

evidence.note: “Let my shoulder fall from the shoulder blade, and my arm (וְאֶזְרֹעִי) be broken from the bone.”

words.summary: Twice: the seed set aside for sowing, and the plants a garden makes to spring up.

senses.definition: Seed for sowing, and what springs from it in a garden.

evidence.note: “If any of their carcass falls on any sowing seed (זֶרַע זֵרוּעַ) which is to be sown, it is clean.”
“As a garden causes the things sown in it (זֵרוּעֶיהָ) to spring up, so the Lord Yahweh will cause righteousness to spring up.”

words.summary: Once, in the plural, in Daniel; the brief also counts Dan 1:16, which has the form זֵרְעֹנִים (next word). What is grown from seed, eaten instead of the king's food.

senses.definition: Food grown from seed, set against the king's meat and wine.

evidence.note: “Let them give us vegetables (מִן־הַזֵּרֹעִים) to eat and water to drink.”

words.summary: Once, in the plural, in Daniel: another form of זֵרֹעַ, with the ending ‑ôn (the brief counts Dan 1:12 here too). Syriac zarʿōnā, “grain, seed”, is the same formation.

senses.definition: The vegetables given to Daniel and his companions.

evidence.note: “The steward took away their portion of food and the wine … and gave them vegetables (זֵרְעֹנִים).”

words.summary: Once: the place where seed is sown, with the prefix מִ‑ of place. Punic mzrʿ “sown land” is the same word.

senses.definition: The sown land along the Nile.

evidence.note: “Every sown field of the Nile (מִזְרַע יְאוֹר) shall wither, be driven away, and be no more.”

words.summary: Once in Daniel's Aramaic, with z as in the Hebrew (Jewish Aramaic has both זְרַע and דְּרַע).

senses.definition: The seed of men: the kingdoms of the feet mingle by marriage and do not hold together.

evidence.note: “They shall mingle themselves with the seed of men (בִּזְרַע אֲנָשָׁא), but they shall not cleave one to another, as iron does not mix with clay.”

words.summary: Daniel's Aramaic word for the arm, spelled with ד where Hebrew has ז, as Aramaic does for an older ḏ. The z cognates of “sow” count against it as against Hebrew זְרוֹעַ: another older root.

senses.definition: The arms of the image.

evidence.note: “Its breast and its arms (וּדְרָעוֹהִי) of silver.”

words.summary: Once, in Ezra's Aramaic: the arm as force, with prefixed א as in Hebrew אֶזְרוֹעַ and Jewish Aramaic אֶדְרַע. The z cognates of “sow” count against it as against Hebrew זְרוֹעַ: another older root.

senses.definition: Force of arms used to stop the building.

evidence.note: “They went in haste to Jerusalem to the Jews, and made them cease by arm and power (בְּאֶדְרָע וְחָיִל).”

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܙܪܥ (zraʿ), for σπείρω: the sower of the parables, the law of sowing and reaping, and the dead “sown” in the ground.

senses.definition: To sow seed, and figuratively to sow to the flesh or to the spirit and reap accordingly.

evidence.note: “The sower (זָרֻועָא) went out to sow (דּנֵזרֻוע).”
“He who sowed the good seed is the Son of man.”
“What a man sows (דּזָרַע), that he reaps.”
“He who gives seed to the sower (לזָרֻועָא).”

senses.definition: Of the dead body, laid in the ground to be raised.

evidence.note: “They are sown (מֵזדַּרעִינ) in corruption; they rise without corruption.”

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܙܪܥܐ (zarʿā), for σπέρμα: the seed sown in the parables and the seed of Abraham and of David.

senses.definition: Seed for sowing; in the parable, the good seed are the sons of the kingdom.

evidence.note: “The good seed (זַרעָא דֵּינ טָבָֿא) are the sons of the kingdom.”

senses.definition: The descendants, and the one descendant, to whom the promises were made.

evidence.note: “To Abraham and to his seed (וַלזַרעֵה) … ‘to your seed’, as of one, who is the Messiah.”
“If you are the Messiah's, then you are the seed of Abraham and heirs by the promise.”
“Born in the flesh of the seed (זַרעָא) of the house of David.”
“The children of the promise are counted for seed.”

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܕܪܥܐ (drāʿā), for βραχίων: the arm of God at the exodus and in Isa 53:1. The z cognates of “sow” count against it as against Hebrew זְרוֹעַ: another older root.

senses.definition: God's arm, his power at work.

evidence.note: Isa 53:1: “the arm of the Lord (וַדֿרָעֵה דּמָריָא), to whom has it been revealed?”
“With a high arm (ובַֿדֿרָעָא רָמָא) he brought them out.”
“He has wrought victory with his arm.”

cognates.gloss: sow; seed produce, sown field; offspring; a man's seed
cognates.note: The verb is “he sowed, or cast seed”, with the proverb “he who sows reaps”; زَرْعٌ is what is raised by sowing, and by extension a man's offspring and his seminal fluid, and the harvest of conduct (“very evil is the harvest of the sinner”). Every sense of Hebrew זֶרַע is here. The Arabic has z (ز), not ḏ (ذ).

evidence.note: “He sowed, or cast seed … They say, مَنْ زَرَعَ حَصَدَ [He who sows reaps].”
“Seed-produce; what is raised by means of sowing … Offspring, or children; or a child … The seed, or seminal fluid, of a man.”
“Seed, or grain, for sowing.”
“A place of زَرْع [or seed-produce]”: formed as מִזְרָע.

cognates.note: ذِرَاعٌ is the forearm, and the cubit measured by it; the verbal noun ذَرْعٌ is “the stretching forth … the arm”, and figuratively a man's power or reach: “he lacked strength to do the thing” is literally “his arm was too narrow for it”. The Hebrew arm is likewise strength, and Yahweh's arm is “outstretched”. Arabic ḏ (ذ), not z (ز), stands behind the ז: another older sound from that of زَرَعَ “sow”.

evidence.note: “[The part] from the elbow to the extremities of the fingers; the fore arm … [the space] from the extremity of the elbow to the extremity of the middle finger.”
“In its primary acceptation, signifies The stretching forth, or extending, the arm, or fore leg.”
“Power, or ability; as also ذِرَاعٌ … a man's reach, or extent of power or ability.”

cognates.note: One of the commonest Akkadian nouns, with the Hebrew's range: seed for sowing, sown land, and offspring. Akkadian writes older z and ḏ alike as z, so it does not show which stands behind the ז.

evidence.note: Meanings: seed, grain, offspring, progeny, descendant, field, arable land, sown land, seed-measure; 3,985 instances.

cognates.note: Ugaritic writes the noun with d (𐎄) and has the verb “to sow” (tdrʿnn, of Anat sowing Mot in the field). Ugaritic d for Hebrew z can only stand for an older ḏ (older z stays z in Ugaritic), so Ugaritic points to ḏ for “seed”, against Arabic z. Segert's glossary is read from OCR, which does not keep d and ḏ apart; the form 𐎄 is from Wiktionary.

evidence.locator: Ugaritic 𐎄𐎗𐎓 (drʿ), noun: seed (of a plant)

evidence.note: “tdr‘nn with suff. 3. sing. m. ‘to sow; scatter?’ (cf. H., Anc.-Aram. z-r-ʿ, Arab. zara‘a … Akkad. zarû; cf. also H. Hos 2:25; Lev 25:3)” (OCR read; PDF not rendered).

cognates.note: Written with ḏ (𐎏), the older sound Arabic ḏirāʿ also shows.

evidence.note: An entry “arm” with Hebrew, Aramaic, Syriac and Arabic comparisons; the OCR garbles its letters, and the reading is not checked against the PDF.

cognates.note: In Phoenician curses and prayers from Byblos and Karatepe: “may you not have seed among the living under the sun”, “may they have neither son nor seed in their stead”, “may I and my seed gain good things”. The sense is the Hebrew's “offspring”. Phoenician z covers older z and ḏ alike.

evidence.note: “[Heb. zera‘] n.m. SEED, OFFSPRING … ‘And may they shall not have son nor seed to replace them [lit., in their stead]!’ … ‘May I and my seed gain acquisitions and good things!’” (OCR read; the page break falls near the entry).

cognates.note: Neo-Punic, Mactar: “we possessed sown land and abundance”: the same formation as מִזְרָע.

evidence.note: “[Heb. mizraʿ] n.m. SOWN LAND, CULTIVATED SOIL” (OCR read).

cognates.note: The Syriac root of sowing, with z, where Syriac writes the arm drāʿā with d: Syriac keeps the two apart as Arabic does. zarʿōnā is formed as Hebrew זֵרְעֹן. The Peshitta's uses are entered as words of this entry.

evidence.locator: lexemes 913 ZRE, sow; 914 ZREA, seed; 915 ZREONA, grain, seed; 912 ZROEA, sower (root 580 ZRE)

cognates.note: Syriac d answers to an older ḏ, as in Arabic ḏirāʿ.
The Targums' verb and noun with z: Onkelos at Gen 1:11 for the seed of herbs, and the Targum of Judges 6:3 for Israel's sowing.

evidence.note: The Aramaic verb of זָרַע, to sow; Targ. Jud. VI, 3; participle זָרֵעַ, Targ. Prov. XI, 18.
The Aramaic noun of זֶרַע, seed; Targ. O. Gen. I, 11.

cognates.note: Beside זְרַע the Targums also write the sowing words with d (Targ. Koh. 2:5; Targ. Y. Gen. 4:3), the Aramaic reflex of an older ḏ. With Ugaritic drʿ this points to ḏ for “seed” as well as for “arm”, against Arabic and Syriac z.

evidence.note: “= זְרַע to sow. Targ. Koh. II, 5. Targ. Job XXXI, 8 Ms. (ed. זרע).”
“seed, produce; offspring. Targ. Y. Gen. IV, 3 … Targ. Cant. I, 14.”

cognates.note: The Targums' word for Hebrew זְרוֹעַ, as at Exo 6:6 and the shoulder of Num 6:19, also with prefixed א (Targ. Jer. 32:21, for Hebrew אֶזְרוֹעַ).

evidence.note: “= h., arm, (of animals) shoulder. Targ. Ex. VI, 6. Targ. O. Num. VI, 19.”
“(= h. אֶזְרוֹעַ, v. זְרוֹעַ) arm. Targ. Jer. XXXII, 21.”

cognates.note: Ge'ez has both senses of the Hebrew noun. Ge'ez writes older z and ḏ alike as z. From Wiktionary only; Dillmann not yet checked.

evidence.locator: Ge'ez ዘርእ (zärʾ), noun: seed; issue, offspring, progeny

doctrine.statement: After the transgression Yahweh God said to the serpent, “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; he shall strike your head, and you shall strike his heel” (Gen 3:15). The word is the one used for a son (Eve calls Seth “another seed instead of Abel”, Gen 4:25), and the one who strikes the head is “he”, one of the woman's seed. The serpent's seed are men of the serpent's mind: John and Jesus called the Pharisees “offspring of vipers” (Mat 3:7; 23:33), and Jesus told those who sought to kill him, “you are of your father the false accuser” (Jhn 8:44). Paul says God sent his son “born of a woman” (Gal 4:4); Hebrews, that since the children share flesh and blood he also shared the same, “that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the false accuser” (Heb 2:14); and Paul tells the believers, “the God of peace will crush the adversary under your feet shortly” (Rom 16:20). From the verses: the seed of the woman is a man, Jesus, born of a woman and sharing the nature of those he saves; his heel was struck when he died, and by that death and his rising he destroyed the power of death, the serpent's head, in a victory his brethren will share.

Yahweh promised Abram the land “to your seed” (Gen 12:7), “to you and to your seed for ever” (Gen 13:15), and swore after the offering of Isaac, “your seed shall possess the gate of his enemies, and in your seed shall all the nations of the earth bless themselves” (Gen 22:17–18). The noun is singular and can stand for a multitude (“so shall your seed be”, like the stars, Gen 15:5) or for one son (Gen 4:25; 21:13); in Gen 22:17 the seed possesses the gate of “his” enemies. Paul reads the promise of one: “He does not say ‘and to seeds’, as of many, but as of one, ‘and to your seed’, which is Christ” (Gal 3:16); and then, “if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal 3:29), those baptized into Christ having put on Christ (Gal 3:27). Peter says the blessing of the nations in Abraham's seed came when God raised up his servant Jesus and sent him “to bless you, in turning away every one of you from your iniquities” (Act 3:25–26). Descent alone does not make the seed: “in Isaac shall your seed be called … the children of the promise are counted for seed” (Rom 9:7–8, quoting Gen 21:12), and Jesus told men who were Abraham's seed by birth that Abraham's children would do Abraham's works (Jhn 8:37–39). The promise to Abraham and his seed was “that he should be heir of the world” (Rom 4:13), yet Abraham and his sons died in faith without receiving it, that they should not be made perfect without us (Heb 11:13, 39–40). From the verses: the seed is first Christ, and then all who are in him by faith and baptism, Jew or Gentile; the blessing is the forgiveness of sins through him; and the inheritance, the land and the world, is still to be received, together, at the resurrection.

Yahweh promised David by Nathan, “I will raise up your seed after you, who shall come out of your body, and I will establish his kingdom … I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (2Sa 7:12–14). The psalm repeats it, “your seed I will establish for ever, and build up your throne to all generations”, “his seed shall be for ever, and his throne as the sun before me” (Psa 89:5, 37); and when the throne was cut off from Coniah's line (Jer 22:30), Jeremiah still promised that Yahweh would multiply the seed of David and take rulers from it over the seed of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Jer 33:22, 26). Hebrews applies “I will be to him a father” to Jesus (Heb 1:5). The angel told Mary that the power of the Most High would overshadow her, so that the child would be called the son of God, and that God would give him “the throne of his father David”, to reign over the house of Jacob for ever (Luk 1:32–35). Paul says God raised up to Israel “of this man's seed, according to promise, a saviour, Jesus” (Act 13:23), “made of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom 1:3; 2Ti 2:8), as the people knew the Christ must be (Jhn 7:42). From the verses: Jesus is David's seed by his birth from Mary and God's son because God himself begot him; he is a man, as the promise required, and the throne he is to receive is David's throne, over the house of Jacob, in a kingdom that will have no end.

A man's arm is his strength (1Sa 2:31), and to trust in man is to “make flesh his arm” (Jer 17:5; 2Ch 32:8). Yahweh's arm is his own strength put forth: by it he made the heavens and the earth (Jer 32:17), and brought Israel out of Egypt “with a strong hand and an outstretched arm” (Deu 26:8; Exo 6:6). Isaiah says that when Yahweh saw there was no man and no one to intercede, “his own arm brought salvation to him” (Isa 59:16; 63:5); that “Yahweh has bared his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God” (Isa 52:10); and then asks, “Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed?”, and describes the servant, despised and rejected, who poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa 53:1, 3, 12). John quotes the question of the unbelief that met Jesus' signs (Jhn 12:37–38), and Peter calls Jesus “a man approved of God among you by mighty works and wonders and signs, which God did by him” (Act 2:22). From the verses: the arm of Yahweh is not another beside him but his own power, and it was revealed in a man, his servant, through whom God himself worked salvation.

Yahweh speaks of sowing his people: “I will sow her for myself in the land” (Hos 2:25), and “I will sow them among the peoples … and they shall live” (Zec 10:9). Paul answers the question “How are the dead raised?” from sowing: “what you sow is not made alive unless it dies”, and “it is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption … it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body” (1Co 15:36, 42–44). The raising is at Christ's coming, “at the last trumpet; for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible” (1Co 15:23, 52), and until then “the dead know nothing” (Ecc 9:5). From the verses: man is mortal; the dead lie in the ground like sown seed, without life or knowledge, and live again only when they are raised at Christ's return, changed to incorruption.

The farmer reaps what he sowed, and the prophets and wise men make it a law of judgment: “they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind” (Hos 8:7); “sow for yourselves in righteousness, reap according to covenant faithfulness” (Hos 10:12); “he who sows iniquity shall reap calamity” (Pro 22:8); “those who sow in tears shall reap with a joyful shout” (Psa 126:5). Paul states it of the judgment to come: “whatever a man sows, that he shall also reap; for he who sows to his own flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption, but he who sows to the spirit shall of the spirit reap everlasting life” (Gal 6:7–8). From the verses: everlasting life is not possessed by nature but reaped as a harvest by those who have sown to the spirit, and corruption is the harvest of the flesh.

note: Drafted 2026-11-15. Root: the brief's key זרע, which BDB uses for both “sow” (g.cl) and “arm” (g.cm); no other entry had it. One spelling, two older roots? Arabic keeps them apart (زرع zaraʿa “sow” with z; ذراع ḏirāʿ “arm” with ḏ), and Syriac likewise (zraʿ with z, drāʿā with d), so the arm words name ḏ cognates and the seed words z cognates. But the evidence for “seed” is not clean: Ugaritic writes the noun drʿ with d (which can only be older ḏ beside Hebrew z) and Jewish Aramaic has דְּרַע beside זְרַע for sow and seed, so lexicon-splits will show the seed words with both z and ḏ. Whether “seed” was *ḏrʿ with Arabic z irregular, or *zrʿ with the Ugaritic and Targum d forms secondary, is left open; arm is ḏ throughout. Akkadian, Phoenician and Ge'ez write z for both and give no sound. The Ugaritic d/ḏ distinction is taken from Wiktionary's forms; Segert's OCR does not keep them apart (PDF not rendered). Krahmalkov's ZRʿ falls at a page break (pp. 172–173 in the OCR). Words: the brief's “(no stem)” tokens under the verb key g.cl.aa (Gen 1:29b; 15:3; 19:32, 34; 21:12; Lev 15:16–18; 22:4; 26:5; Num 5:28; Ezk 17:5) are the noun זֶרַע by spelling and are cited under the noun; Jdg 6:3 under the noun key is the verb. g.cl.ad and g.cl.ae each list both Dan 1:12 and 1:16; each word is given its own verse. Aramaic דְּרָע (xd.ao.ab) and אֶדְרָע (xd.ao.ac) are not in the זרע brief (they are keyed under דרע and אדרע) and are added here with their own roots. Left out: יִזְרְעֶאל (g.cl.af), for the name entry names/jezreel.json, which also takes the gentilic יִזְרְעֵאלִי (g.cl.ag); a.ci.ac, j.bd.ae and m.bj.ag are cross-references with no tokens; g.cm.aa is BDB's heading for “arm” and xd.ao.aa for Aramaic דרע, with no tokens. The place Edrei (אֶדְרֶעִי, d.cj.ab, filed under דרע) is not taken: a place name whose link to the root is unproven. Zerubbabel (זְרֻבָּבֶל, xg.ai.ab, its own root key) has no name entry: scripture does not explain the name, and the reading Akkadian zēr-Bābili “seed of Babylon” is a lead with no source checked here. Leads not followed: Akkadian izīru “(upper) arm” (Oracc armep x000044470, Neo-Assyrian) as a possible cognate of the arm; Akkadian zarû “scatter, winnow; sow” is the root of Hebrew זָרָה and is not cited; Ge'ez mäzraʿt “arm” and Sabaean forms (Wiktionary, Biella) not checked; Payne Smith for the Syriac senses; the Septuagint's γένος and σπορά for זֶרַע not traced. Psalm references use the Hebrew verse numbers (Psa 89:5, 30, 37 are English 89:4, 29, 36); Hos 2:25 is English 2:23.
